author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A complete sentence has a subject (who or what it is about) and a verb (what the subject does or is), and it makes a full thought. Example: The cat sleeps.
title: A sentence

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Start every sentence with a capital letter. Also capitalize names of people, places and days, and the word I. Example: Cory lives in Texas.
title: Capital letters

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: End a statement with a period, a question with a question mark, and a strong feeling with an exclamation mark.
title: Ending punctuation

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Use commas to separate three or more items in a list. Example: I like apples, bananas, and grapes.
title: Commas in a list

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: An apostrophe shows missing letters in a contraction. Do not becomes don't. It is becomes it's. I am becomes I'm.
title: Apostrophes for contractions

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: An apostrophe plus s shows ownership. The dog's bone is the bone that belongs to the dog.
title: Apostrophes for ownership

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: It's means it is or it has. Its shows ownership, like its tail. Example: It's a cat, and its tail is long.
title: Its and it's (apostrophe confusion)

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Their shows ownership. There points to a place. They're means they are. Example: They're over there with their dog.
title: Their, there and they're

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: To is a direction or part of a verb, too means also or very, and two is the number 2. Example: I want to go too, and I have two tickets.
title: To, too and two

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Your shows ownership. You're means you are. Example: You're holding your book.
title: Your and you're

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Examples: girl, park, dragon, kindness.
title: Nouns

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A verb is an action or a state of being. Examples: run, think, is, are.
title: Verbs

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: An adjective describes a noun. Examples: small, purple, brave. In a brave small dragon, brave and small are adjectives.
title: Adjectives

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb, and often ends in ly. Example: She sang loudly.
title: Adverbs

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A pronoun takes the place of a noun. Examples: he, she, it, they, we, you, I. Example: Zeref is small, and he is brave.
title: Pronouns

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Add s to make most nouns plural: cat becomes cats. Add es after s, x, ch or sh: box becomes boxes. Some are irregular: child becomes children, mouse becomes mice, foot becomes feet.
title: Singular and plural

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Add ed to most verbs to show the past: walk becomes walked. Some are irregular: go becomes went, run becomes ran, see becomes saw, eat becomes ate.
title: Past tense

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb. The dog runs. The dogs run.
title: Subject and verb agreement

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Use an before a vowel sound and a before a consonant sound. An apple, a banana, an hour, a unicorn.
title: A and an

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Use who for the person doing the action and whom for the person receiving it. Who wrote the letter? To whom did you give it?
title: Who and whom

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Use fewer with things you can count and less with amounts you cannot count. Fewer cookies, less water.
title: Fewer and less

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Synonyms are words with nearly the same meaning. Happy and joyful are synonyms. Big and huge are synonyms.
title: Synonyms

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings. Hot and cold are antonyms. Up and down are antonyms.
title: Antonyms

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings and spellings. Sea and see, red and read, hear and here.
title: Homophones

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. Start a new paragraph when the idea changes.
title: Paragraphs

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Polite words: please when you ask, thank you when you receive, excuse me to get attention, and sorry when you make a mistake.
title: Greeting and thanks

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Questions often start with who, what, where, when, why or how, and end with a question mark. Example: Where is the moon?
title: Questions

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: Quotation marks surround the exact words someone says. Example: Zeref said, Rawr.
title: Quotation marks

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A helpful rule: i before e, except after c, as in receive. There are exceptions such as weird and science.
title: Spelling i before e

author: Grok Bot for Cory Davis, original 2026-10-26 (authored for this bank; no copied text)
text: A good short answer is a full sentence that answers the question first and then adds one helpful detail if needed.
title: Short good answer
